# 0066: A lease reports its nameservers

Status: accepted
Date: 2026-08-03
Milestone: the half [0065](0065-udhcpc-needs-a-script-and-netcfgd-writes-it.md) left

## Context

`config = "dhcp"` gave an address and a route and no DNS. Neither client told
netcfgd what nameservers the lease carried, so a laptop that followed the first-run
guide -- which recommends `global { dns { mode = "write_resolv_conf" } }` -- got
this:

```
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by netcfgd. Edits will be overwritten.
```

**netcfgd overwrote a working resolver file with one that resolves nothing**, and
`ncfg plan` said `dns.apply` and warned only that it could not be undone. Measured,
not inferred.

## Decision

**Both clients run a netcfgd-generated script that writes the lease's nameservers
into the interface report.** The report contract
([doc/interface-report.md](../interface-report.md)) already has a `dns` key, and
[0049](0049-a-server-may-name-resolvers-not-where-queries-go.md) already has the
gate, so **no new mechanism and no new gate** were needed -- only the reporting half
that 0049 left for later. udhcpc's script gained a `report` function; dhcpcd gets a
script of its own through `-c`, which the man page of the version in Debian confirms
replaces `/usr/lib/dhcpcd/dhcpcd-run-hooks`.

An operator takes the lease's servers the way 0049's third row already says:

```
global { dns { mode = "write_resolv_conf" } }

interface eth0 {
	config = "dhcp"
	dns    { }          # yes, use what this network hands out
}
```

An empty `dns { }` block is the whole opt-in. Without it the servers are reported
and not delivered, which is 0049 holding: a remote party may name resolvers, and
whether this machine uses them is the operator's to write down.

**A domain is a comment and never a key**, in both scripts, which is 0049's other
half: `search`/`domain` is a decision about which names go where, and there is no
report key for one. What the server said is written into the file where a person can
read it and netcfgd's parser drops it.

## And it ends a fight nobody had noticed

dhcpcd's own `20-resolv.conf` hook writes `/etc/resolv.conf`, directly or through
`resolvconf` -- read out of the shipped hook, not assumed. So on any machine where
netcfgd's DNS mode owns that file, **both were writing it and whichever ran last
won.** Passing `-c` replaces dhcpcd's whole hook directory, which ends that. It is
also why netcfgd's script is not a file dropped into `dhcpcd-hooks/`: netcfgd writes
nothing outside `/run` but the DNS artifacts, and a hook directory in `/usr/lib` is
the distribution's.

Two more things dhcpcd's default hooks were doing that now stop:

- **`30-hostname`** sets the hostname from the lease when the current one is blank
  or `localhost`. 0061 refuses `hostname = "dhcp"` on the grounds that a machine's
  identity is not a remote server's to change; leaving dhcpcd to do it anyway would
  have been that decision holding in the config and not in fact.
- **Everything else in the directory**, which is the honest cost of `-c` and is
  named here rather than discovered: `ntp.conf`, `yp.conf` and the rest are no
  longer written. A machine that wanted them wants a decision about which of them
  netcfgd should report, not a silent restoration.

## A resolver file with nothing in it says so

Independently of DHCP: when every DNS scope has a mode and no servers, the plan now
warns, and where a report offered servers nothing asked for it names the interface
and the one-line fix. Warned rather than refused -- the operator asked netcfgd to
own the file, and leaving a stale one behind is drift the config cannot describe --
but the silence is gone.

The first version of that check fired on **every** document that manages no DNS at
all, because `all` on an empty list is true. Two existing fixtures caught it, both
asserting that a converged plan warns about nothing.

## Consequences

- `config = "dhcp"` plus `dns { }` resolves names, with either client.
- The report is the only path, so a modem helper, a tunnel and a DHCP lease all
  arrive the same way and 0049's gate governs all three. Nothing about DHCP is
  special-cased in the planner.
- The lease's servers arrive on the apply *after* the one that started the client,
  because that is when the report exists -- the same asynchrony the `lease` hook has
  (0064). The live test asserts the intermediate state rather than hiding it.
- `tests/live/dhcp.sh` covers it end to end: a real `busybox udhcpd` sending a
  nameserver and a domain, netcfgd's script reporting both, the server reaching
  `resolv.conf`, the domain staying a comment, and -- with the `dns { }` block
  removed -- the plan saying why the file would resolve nothing.
- `+8 KB` installed.

## What is left

**A lease's `search` domain is still nowhere.** `search` is suffix completion, not
query routing, so unlike `domains` it is not the thing 0049 refuses -- it could
honestly become a report key. It is not one today, and adding it is a change to a
document marked "stable, this is a contract", which wants its own decision rather
than a line in this one.

**dhcpcd's script is untested against dhcpcd**, which is not installed on the
machine this was written on. Its shape was read out of dhcpcd 10.1.0's own
`20-resolv.conf` and its `-c` option out of its man page, and the generated text is
checked by `sh -n` and by assertions on what it must not contain -- but no dhcpcd
has run it. `tests/live/dhcp.sh` drives the busybox half; the dhcpcd half needs a
machine with the package, and that is the honest gap.
